items.title: Pro-Life Group Reportedly Kicked Out of Coffee Shop, Compared to KKK
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: The founder of a well-known pro-life organization has gone viral in recent days after reportedly being kicked out of an […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

The founder of a well-known pro-life organization has gone viral in recent days after reportedly being kicked out of an Idaho coffee shop after the owner learned she was holding a meeting there.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Kristan Hawkins, president of Students for Life of America, shared a video of what purportedly took place at Wydaho Roasters last month — and that video went viral.

Hawkins told CBN News that coffee shop owner Jim Sheehan made his displeasure known after she, her son, and others met to discuss pro-life issues inside Wydaho Roasters. Her son’s goal has been to rally people against Proposition 1, an abortion measure that will be on the ballot in November.

“We’re recruiting door knockers, and we’ve had students going door to door, educating people in Idaho about this extreme abortion ballot referendum, which sadly many people don’t know about,” Hawkins said, noting her son rallied people online to come meet to form a pro-life group to address the issue.

The coffee shop was the intended gathering place for the group’s first meeting, but that didn’t go very well.

“We had purchased our drinks and our food,” she said. “Some other leaders, community members, came to kind of join the group that I knew from church.”

According to Hawkins, Sheehan came out of his office and told the group they couldn’t meet at the shop and needed to leave. Hawkins took out her camera and started filming the interaction, hoping she could simply convince the owner to let them stay for the first meeting and then pledge not to return.

“I was trying to negotiate with him, just like, let us finish this meeting; we won’t come back,” she said. “And then he just kept going and then compared us to the KKK and said, we were like the KKK, that pro-lifers were like the KKK, which was just beyond the pale. And that’s actually why I decided to release the video.”

Hawkins made it clear that she believes, as an owner, Sheehan has the right to refuse service and was within his rights to ask the group to leave. That said, she also believes in her right to expose his purported comparison between the pro-life activists and the KKK.

The result of the entire escapade was intense media coverage and viral video discussion. Ultimately, both Hawkins and Sheehan reportedly started getting death threats.

“He was well within his rights to kick us out,” Hawkins said. “I was within my rights to expose his insanity, believing that community members were like the KKK, but neither of us deserves to die or receive death threats.”

Sheehan told Fox News that he pushes back on claims the group was kicked out. He said he had asked via Facebook the day before that the group not meet in his coffee shop.

“Sunday she announced on a local community page they were holding this meeting at our business, naming it — I responded to the post politely asking them not to use our business as the agenda of the organization does not align with us,” he told the outlet. “They showed up anyway.”

items.title: Christian Grandma Refuses to Back Down After Government Demands She Stop Feeding Community
items.author: Billy Hallowell
items.summary: What started as a woman feeling called to cook breakfast for a handful of friends has turned into a dispute […]
items.content:
📖 News | Faithwire

What started as a woman feeling called to cook breakfast for a handful of friends has turned into a dispute over food, faith, and government regulations.

Listen to the latest episode of “Quick Start”

Kathy Kite, a resident of Harrisburg, Missouri, began welcoming locals into her home for breakfast back in May after the community’s convenience store stopped serving breakfast following COVID.

Kite works at H-Town, the local convenience store and gas station, and said residents had repeatedly expressed interest in finding a new place to have breakfast. She lives nearby, so she decided to offer an alternative by cooking for her friends and offering up the food for free.

“I told the old guys that come in there in the mornings that like to play cards, and drink coffee, and eat breakfast, and say they didn’t have any more — I’m like, ‘You guys can come to my house and I’ll do it,’” Kite told CBN News.

So, she started offering breakfast out of her kitchen and people came.

“It all started with just some like sausage, egg, and cheese biscuits,” Kite said.

At first, it was just a few people. But others soon began to come after her loving act was advertised on social media, with 20-25 people regularly coming to her home in the morning; some parents even brought their kids to her house for food before school. Kite gets up at 3:30 a.m. to prepare for the day.

“And it just kind of exploded from there,” Kite said. “So then people were like, ‘Breakfast? We have breakfast in town?’”

Kite doesn’t charge for the meals. There is a place for people to leave money if they choose, but she said those contributions go back into buying ingredients and food.

“It’s not a moneymaker by any means,” she said.

For Kite, feeding people is also deeply connected to her Christian faith.

“For whatever reason, God has put it in my heart that I need to take care of people,” she said. “I like to feed people.”

Kite continued, “In my mind feeding people is loving people.”

But Kite’s breakfast gatherings eventually caught the attention of government officials, with Columbia city officials from the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department reportedly sending a letter telling her she needed a commercial kitchen license to continue operating.

Kite disputes that she is operating a business, though, and said the government’s demands have broken her heart.

“I’m not running a business,” she said. “This is just friends coming over for breakfast. It’s no different than a backyard barbecue or a church gathering.”

Kite said the warning dramatically affected attendance, as some residents became concerned that continuing to visit could cause additional trouble for her. As a result, many stopped coming.

“I went from having probably 20 to 25 to maybe 5 to 8 people,” she said.

Still, Kite isn’t planning to stop, despite admitting she was scared to incur fines or worse. Rather than back down, she sought legal help and has no plans to stop.

“God laid this on me and I just feel like if God brought me to it, God’s going to bring me through it,” Kite said. “I believe in what I’m doing. I don’t believe I’m doing anything wrong.”

The Goldwater Institute is helping Kite and has sent a letter to the Boone County health department seeking answers about why they are demanding a commercial kitchen. Officials with the Columbia/Boone County Public Health and Human Services Department told Fox News that Kite has a tip jar, open sign, and is advertising food on social media, indicating elements “associated with a food establishment.”

“No citations or cease-and-desist orders were issued. We also did not threaten jail time,” the statement read. “We sent a letter to Ms. Kite following a complaint we received that food served in her establishment made someone ill. Our role in public health is to work with food establishments to promote safe food practices and prevent food-borne illnesses.”

The text continued, “There are safe, allowable ways to provide homemade food to the community with and without a food permit. We regularly work together with individuals and businesses who want to provide free food to the community.”

items.title: The Celebrity Pastor Era Finally Ended. But Then Christian Influencers Took Its Spot.
items.author: Annie Eisner
items.summary: The American church has always had a thing for celebrity — but something shifted over the past five years. We used to point to cool megachurch pastors befriending high-profile believers as proof that Christianity still had cultural pull. Then came a stretch of very public pastoral scandals — resigna
items.content:
📖 Culture | Relevant Magazine

The American church has always had a thing for celebrity — but something shifted over the past five years.

We used to point to cool megachurch pastors befriending high-profile believers as proof that Christianity still had cultural pull. Then came a stretch of very public pastoral scandals — resignations, affairs, whole ministries unraveling in real time — and the shine wore off fast.

The allure of charismatic pastors in designer clothes started to feel less like access and more like a mirage. For a generation already skeptical of institutions, the curtain had been pulled back on the Celebrity Pastor Industrial Complex.

Beaty is careful not to vilify the instinct. “Celebrities need Jesus too, so I’m sure there are very good things about these friendships,” she said of celebrity believers. “We attach to them, in part because it lends credibility to a faith that seems weird to a lot of our neighbors. We want to feel like, ‘See? We’re not that weird.’ It lends cultural credibility to our faith.”

But while one kind of platform crumbled, another rose. In place of celebrity pastors, today we have the Christian influencer.

These are people who might not lead a church or hold theological degrees, but they rack up millions of views by talking about God online. Whether it’s an aesthetic devotional or a car confessional, they’re massively popular.

“There’s been a significant decline in trust in institutions,” said author Katelyn Beaty, whose book Celebrities for Jesus explores how platform culture has changed the American church. “In their place, I think many Americans are predisposed to attach themselves to individual figures, most of whom they’ve never encountered in any personal way. But these individuals come to not only symbolize some kind of value or aspiration or political ideology, but also a theological flavor.”

Social media makes these relationships feel personal — like the audience actually knows these people, can trust them, can build a spiritual framework around their content.

But influence doesn’t always mean formation, and visibility doesn’t guarantee wisdom. Many of these creators are new to faith themselves — sincere, maybe even inspiring, but not elders, not pastors, and not accountable to anyone.

“Because of the spiritual emphases of the evangelical movement, there tends to be a distrust of institutions,” Beaty said. “You have to have this born again, highly individualistic experience of salvation, and that often comes through the preaching of a specific evangelist or writer. So I think it is something in the water in American evangelicalism, that we are suspicious of institutions because we don’t really believe they do dynamic work for the Kingdom.”

That suspicion now extends to the church itself — especially among younger Christians who’ve watched spiritual abuse, manipulation or hypocrisy play out up close, and come away disillusioned. Instead of plugging into a church, they log into Instagram or YouTube for spiritual nourishment from someone who feels more relatable, less institutional — more real.

“I wonder if we are actually in a time when the church is going to have to accept becoming smaller and more obscure,” Beaty said. “It’s not going to feel successful. It’s going to feel scary and like maybe God isn’t blessing us.”

But that kind of refinement doesn’t trend. What trends is someone with camera presence, a compelling personal story and the ability to make faith content feel fresh and algorithmically appealing. The line between Christian encouragement and influencer branding blurs — and so does the line between encouragement and authority.

That instinct isn’t inherently bad here either — a video about faith reaching millions of people isn’t a problem on its own. But discipleship doesn’t show up in follower counts or video views.

“So much of the American church has mimicked secular business principles to evaluate success,” Beaty said. “And what we are after, as people attesting to the reality of God in our lives, is not a number of butts in the pews. The metric of discipleship is that you’re actually becoming a community where people are being formed into the likeness of Christ.”

So who is forming us? Who are we actually being discipled by?

If we’re being honest, many of us spend more time listening to Christian influencers than we do talking about our faith in community. We’re not building church families — we’re building an algorithm.

The problem isn’t that influencers talk about Jesus. It’s that we don’t ask who they’re accountable to. We ask how many followers they have. There’s no social media metric for spiritual maturity, and no viral moment that substitutes for long-haul discipleship. There’s no shortcut to Christlikeness — only community, humility and time.

“What if the smaller church and the more localized understanding of Christian discipleship is a way that we are being refined,” Beaty said, “so that the Gospel we attest to actually has staying power and real credibility among our neighbors?”

That’s not glamorous. But it might be the kind of credibility the world actually needs.

items.title: Will the Good of the Other
items.author: Bishop Robert Barron
items.summary:
Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, for this Twenty-second Sunday in Ordinary Time, I want to begin with our very brief second reading from Paul to the Romans.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Bishop Robert Barron

Friends, for this Twenty-second Sunday in Ordinary Time, I want to begin with our very brief second reading from Paul to the Romans. It opens, “I urge you, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God, to offer your bodies as a living sacrifice.” Here we see Christ’s cross and resurrection—the supreme sacrifice fulfilling all the offerings of the temple—extended to all the baptized. The Church is now the place where divinity and humanity are reconciled.

Daily Reading

First Reading
Ezekiel 33:7-9

So you, mortal, I have made a sentinel for the house of Israel; whenever you hear a word from my mouth, you shall give them warning from me. If I say to the wicked, “O wicked ones, you shall surely die,” and you do not speak to warn the wicked to turn from their ways, the wicked shall die in their iniquity, but their blood I will require at your hand. But if you warn the wicked to turn from their ways, and they do not turn from their ways, the wicked shall die in their iniquity, but you will have saved your life.

Psalm
Psalm 95:1-2, 6-7, 8-9

O come, let us sing to the Lord;
    let us make a joyful noise to the rock of our salvation!
Let us come into his presence with thanksgiving;
    let us make a joyful noise to him with songs of praise!
O come, let us worship and bow down,
    let us kneel before the Lord, our Maker!
For he is our God,
    and we are the people of his pasture,
    and the sheep of his hand.
O that today you would listen to his voice!
Do not harden your hearts, as at Meribah,
    as on the day at Massah in the wilderness,
when your ancestors tested me,
    and put me to the proof, though they had seen my work.

Second Reading
Romans 12:1-2

Owe no one anything, except to love one another; for the one who loves another has fulfilled the law. The commandments, “You shall not commit adultery; You shall not murder; You shall not steal; You shall not covet”; and any other commandment, are summed up in this word, “Love your neighbor as yourself.” Love does no wrong to a neighbor; therefore, love is the fulfilling of the law.

Gospel Reading
Matthew 18:15-20

“If another member of the church sins against you, go and point out the fault when the two of you are alone. If the member listens to you, you have regained that one. But if you are not listened to, take one or two others along with you, so that every word may be confirmed by the evidence of two or three witnesses. If the member refuses to listen to them, tell it to the church; and if the offender refuses to listen even to the church, let such a one be to you as a Gentile and a tax collector. Truly I tell you, whatever you bind on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed in heaven. Again, truly I tell you, if two of you agree on earth about anything you ask, it will be done for you by my Father in heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name, I am there among them.”

items.title: Higher Education Manufactured the Perfect DEI Martyr
items.author: Dr. Matthew Petrusek
items.summary:
Dr. Matthew Petrusek

Jason Arday benefited the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion cult on his way up. But he’s now worth more than ever to them on his way out.
items.content:
📖 Catholic Teaching | Word on Fire

Dr. Matthew Petrusek

The Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion (DEI) craze has produced massive casualties. Cambridge professor Jason Arday is the latest.

Arday took his life amid revelations of a long history of academic plagiarism and biographical fabrication. His death is tragic, especially since he leaves behind a wife and children. But the scandal that preceded it was entirely avoidable.

Critics of DEI have rightly focused on its victims. These include both individuals—mostly white men who lost jobs or were denied promotions—and society as a whole in the form of lower performance standards in vital industries like healthcare, aviation, and public safety.

Yet DEI also harms its beneficiaries. It not only denies their individuality by dissolving them into an abstraction for political gain. It also sets them up for ruin.

Every position has objective qualifications. People either meet those standards or they don’t. This includes academia. Good teaching, scholarship, and research have impartial criteria no matter the discipline. Responsible academics—they still exist, though far too few speak up—know the difference between an excellent scholar, a mediocre scholar, and someone who can’t make the cut.

Arday’s applications should never have passed initial screenings. The fact that he was eventually given tenure and touted as “the best in the world” beggars belief.

Setting aside the plagiarism and outlandish personal claims, a perusal of his work reveals that he cannot clearly communicate ideas or explain how concepts logically relate to each other. That’s like being a pitcher who can’t throw a strike or a pilot who can’t land a plane. The most basic elements of being a professor lay beyond his reach.

Pointing out this lack of competency is not a moral judgment. Arday is responsible for lying, stealing others’ work, and calling the police on the journalist investigating his fraudulent output. But he’s not responsible for getting into a PhD program, landing a plum job, and then becoming a celebrated icon among the cultural elite. That fault belongs to Liverpool John Moores University, which granted him a doctorate on a plagiarized dissertation with a grammatical error in the title; Cambridge University, which awarded him a full professorship when he was thirty-seven years old; and every other institution that uncritically promoted him, like the BBC.

Nobody would know Arday’s name, and he would likely still be alive, if any of these places had simply and quietly said, “Thank you for your interest, but this submission does not meet our standards,” at any point during his manufactured career arc.

But like a child emperor being feted at court, he was lauded every step of the way.

Who benefits from this systemic failure? Certainly not the students, who could tell Arday didn’t have a clue what he was talking about. Certainly not the institutions that now have to explain why anyone should take them seriously. And certainly not Arday himself, whose professional life and personal reputation were always living on borrowed time, just one easy discovery away from total collapse.

The only “winners” from this debacle are the people who raised him up in the first place. They profited from his graduate-student days by telling themselves (and others) that they were giving the right kind of person an opportunity to advance. They profited from his professorship by pedestaling his identity and showing him public homage. And they are still set to literally profit from his life (and death) by selling his biography.
Word on Fire’s Liturgy of the Hours is Here!
Order Your Set Today

The greatest benefit to them, however, is not in his rise to fame, but in his unhappy fall.

The narrative has already formed: He didn’t take his life because he was caught lying, cheating, and seeking to punish others for noticing. He took his life because of, yes, racism.

If the DEI practitioners can get this charge to stick—that it’s not only racist to call out fraud when “marginalized” groups commit it, but also potentially deadly—then they attain an exponentially higher level of immunity from public scrutiny and accountability.

The lesson is thus clear for anyone considering poking around old theses, CVs, and obscure articles looking for more fraud among Arday’s academic collaborators: “Hey bigots, you wouldn’t want another death on your hands, would you? (There’s no telling how our street supporters might respond.)”

Arday benefited the Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion cult on his way up. But he’s now worth more than ever to them on his way out. A DEI martyr, he died so that his crocodile-teared champions may continue enjoying their own unmerited social and economic privileges without being outed as imposters.

DEI didn’t only set Arday up for catastrophic failure. It groomed him into the perfect sacrifice to perpetuate its reign.
